newsitem.title: UK: JPMorgan pioneers euro redenomination in Eurobonds.
newsitem.headline: JPMorgan pioneers euro redenomination in Eurobonds.

text.p: A new clause on an upcoming Eurobond issue allowing future deals to be redenominated in the euro could revolutionise the market, J.P. Morgan officials said on Friday when unveiling the structure.

"The Issuer will have the option to redenominate the Notes in euros. The Notes will be redenominated in such manner as the Issuer...may determine is consistent with existing or anticipated market practice for Eurobonds," the clause read.

J.P. Morgan's head of European capital markets Joe Cook said the above redenomination clause "will make future Eurobonds more liquid than outstanding paper after EMU". He expected the clause would quickly become standard in the Eurobond market.
Qualifying government bonds will be redenominated in euros automatically at the outset of EMU. Outstanding Eurobonds won't.
J.P. Morgan has worked with various sovereign and European institutions and clearing houses on the redenomination project for several months.

Cook told reporters at a news conference: "Parts of the Eurobond market will become fragmented and lose liquidity after EMU while government bonds will be super liquid because of their size and because of the pan-European dimension."

Deals which could become illiquid are existing Eurobonds in currencies which join the single European currency, Cook said. Contractual problems mean these will remain denominated in those currencies, rather then the euro, until 2002.
At the moment European Union law says a borrower must only offer investors the old currency or the euro.
European monetary and economic union is widely expected to go ahead on January 1, 1999. Currencies joining at that stage will remain in partial use until being phased out by 2002.
"Apart from anything else, there is the hidden expense of reprinting and redelivering bonds when redenominating them," Cook said.
The first fruits of redenomination will be seen early next week with the formal launch by Austria, via J.P. Morgan and CDC, of a 3.0-5.0 billion French franc seven-year Eurobond.
Austria will have an option to redenominate the franc bond in euros if and when it and France adopt the currency.
The innovative deal will use English language and law.
Pre-marketing began overnight and the issue was being extremely well received, J.P. Morgan said.
"It will be a benchmark five-year bond in 1999 and is being targeted at institutions," a syndicate manager said.
The Austrian deal, whose coupon and January 2004 maturity exactly match those on an existing Austrian government schilling Bund, has a twist in that it may be exchanged for the Bund.
Investors will be encouraged to exercise their option, the J.P. Morgan syndicate manager said.

Austria may issue further bonds with a 5.50 percent coupon and January 2004 maturity in other core EMU currencies. These deals may also be redenominated in euros by Austria or exchanged into the Austrian bund by investors.
If some investors do not exercise their exchange option, Austria will be allowed to consolidate those bonds, from perhaps several issues, into one jumbo euro Eurobond.
The ultimate aim is to have either a "super liquid Austrian euro Bund or a super liquid euro Eurobond," Cook said.
"Austria is jumping the gun on EMU and taking the initiative in trying to be more investor friendly," Cook said.
"Also, it is a subtle way of exporting its market. French investors will learn about Austrian government bonds."
Austria allows non-resident primary dealers in its domestic government bond market. Cook said that practise must become more widespread as smaller countries battle to attract capital.
"Small countries must take their product to the market."
